extracted.intended_audience: artists, art-critics, and general readers interested in aesthetics and the evaluation of art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for judging whether a work of art is genuine art or a counterfeit, covering essential qualities (transmission of feeling, unity, sincerity, accessibility) and common anti-patterns (borrowing, imitation, effectfulness, 'interestingness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / comprehensibility to all
rubrics_metrics.description: Great works of art are only great because they are accessible and comprehensible to everyone; art's language is understood by all and 'infects all without distinction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: the epic of Genesis, Gospel parables, folk-legends, fairy-tales, folk-songs, story of Joseph, story of Sakya Muni — these transmit very elevated feelings yet remain comprehensible to ordinary people. If a work is incomprehensible to the masses, the conclusion should be that the work is either bad art or not art at all (not that the masses lack taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission (infection) of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of art is to make understood and felt what, in an argument, might be inaccessible; a work of art must 'infect' others with the feelings the artist has experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the artist could have expressed the feeling in words, he would have; art exists because the feeling cannot otherwise be transmitted. A true artistic impression leaves the recipient with the sense that he 'knew the thing before but had been unable to express it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / completeness of form and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief characteristic of a work of art is 'completeness, oneness, the inseparable unity of form and contents expressing the feeling the artist has experienced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that are mere assemblages, borrowed themes mounted by technique, or simulations lack this inseparable unity and therefore cannot produce a real artistic impression. Borrowing whole subjects or features tends to break this unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate emotional effect — art must move people
rubrics_metrics.description: If art fails to move men, it cannot be said that this is due to spectators' lack of understanding; rather, it indicates the work is bad art or not art at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between true infection (sharing an artist's felt emotion) and mere physiological or sensational reactions (see 'striking/effectfulness' anti-pattern). The criterion focuses on real emotional transmission to receivers of ordinary capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / origin in the artist's inner impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal art arises when someone, having experienced a strong emotion, feels the necessity of transmitting it to others; art of the upper classes often lacks this inner impulse and is produced to meet demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True art should spring from the artist's personal experience of feeling, not from an external demand for amusement or remuneration. Professional motives are presented as corrosive of sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not an exercise of the understanding / not requiring specialised preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is differentiated from mental activity that demands preparation and sequence of knowledge by the fact that it acts on people independently of their state of development and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike learning trigonometry after geometry, art should not require prior intellectual training to be felt; requiring 'preparation' is a sign the work is not functioning artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'borrowing' as the basis of art (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing whole subjects or separate features from former works merely recalls earlier impressions and does not transmit the artist's own feeling; such works 'simulate' art rather than create it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: poetical subjects and poetical objects (maidens, moonlight, angels, etc.), Rostand’s Princesse Lointaine as an example of apparently 'poetical' but inauthentic work. Borrowing may pass for art among a perverted taste, but it remains a counterfeit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'imitation' / realism as the measure of art (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating the external details of life—minute description of faces, clothes, gestures, accessories, photographic painting—does not equal art, because such details distract and hinder transmission of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism diverts the receiver's attention to particulars and away from the artist's felt emotion; judging a work by the accuracy of its details is to appraise a counterfeit rather than genuine art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'striking' or effectfulness as substitute for art (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing physical, sensational, or novel effects (contrasts, the horrible, pornographic detail, thunder, crescendos, orchestral crashes) acts on the nerves but does not transmit the artist's feeling and therefore is not art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: detailed descriptions of mutilation, stage devices that produce pity via spectacle (e.g., the play Hannele with staged death and dismal music), program music that attempts to describe non-musical things. Physiological reactions (tears, excitement) can be measured yet are not proof of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'interestingness' (intrigue, novelty, puzzles) as art's criterion (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interestingness—providing new information, intricate plots, or constructing works as riddles to be guessed—distracts the mind and hinders infection; it is not equivalent to artistic impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'interest' comes from unfamiliar factual content or from the pleasure of guessing, that mental effort interferes with feeling transmission. Detailed historical authenticity or puzzle-like construction may create interest but can obstruct art.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a work requires verbal explanation or critical interpretation, it likely fails to infect
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretation of works of art by words indicates that the interpreter is incapable of being infected; if a work needs explanation to be appreciated, it was not successfully transmitting the feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics' explanations are often superfluous and reflect the critics' own insusceptibility; reliance on critics to justify a work's artistic value is a sign of weakness in the work itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware external authority and tradition as sole evaluation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Appraising art by the authority of 'the finest-nurtured' or by canonised traditions (Dante, Raphael, Bach) without an internal standard misleads and produces imitation of masters rather than original art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical tradition can ossify taste and provoke artists to copy celebrated models, producing cold, imitative works (examples: Pushkin later writing a colder Boris Godunoff under critical influence). External precedent should not replace the internal criterion of religious perception/feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary conditions for producing true art
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce real art, an artist must (1) stand on the level of the highest life-conception of his time, (2) experience feeling and have the desire and capacity to transmit it, and (3) possess a talent for some form of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions are seldom combined. Talent alone (ability to express thoughts, notice details, draw, play instruments) without the life-conception and felt experience will typically allow production of counterfeits rather than true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalisation, remuneration, criticism, and schools as causes of counterfeit art
rubrics_metrics.description: The professionalisation of artists (remuneration), the rise of art criticism, and art schools cooperate to cause production and diffusion of counterfeit art by encouraging art made for market demand rather than inner impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional artists must continually invent or supply subjects and may resort to formulaic 'recipes' (borrowing, imitation, effects, interestingness). Criticism and schools can perpetuate imitation by promoting models and external criteria.
